name: Eton Park

summary.text: Eton Park Capital Management was a New York hedge fund founded by former Goldman Sachs partner Eric Mindich. Bloomberg Markets reported in November 2011 that on July 21, 2008 Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson met about a dozen hedge fund managers at Eton Park's Manhattan offices, including Mindich and at least five Goldman Sachs alumni, and described a possible 'conservatorship' of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac that would effectively wipe out common and preferred shareholders, seven weeks before the government did so. No charges were brought; commentators disagreed on whether the disclosures were improper.

sources.title: How Paulson Gave Hedge Funds Advance Word of Fannie Mae Rescue
Paulson Hedge-Fund Chat Not a Crime: William D. Cohan

facts.claim: Bloomberg Markets reported that on July 21, 2008 Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson met about a dozen people at Eton Park's Manhattan offices, including the fund's founder Eric Mindich, and that at least five attendees were alumni of Goldman Sachs, where Paulson had been chief executive.
facts.quote: At least five of them were alumni of Goldman Sachs Group Inc., where Paulson had led the firm.

sources.title: How Paulson Gave Hedge Funds Advance Word of Fannie Mae Rescue

facts.claim: According to a fund manager who attended, Paulson described a path to 'conservatorship' for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and indicated that the companies' common and preferred stock would be effectively wiped out; the government placed both into conservatorship seven weeks later.
facts.quote: Paulson described a path to "conservatorship," a government seizure designed to let the firms keep operating despite heavy mortgage losses.

sources.title: How Paulson Gave Hedge Funds Advance Word of Fannie Mae Rescue

facts.claim: Bloomberg reported that shortly before the meeting Paulson had told the New York Times that regulators' inspections would signal confidence in the two companies, a message that differed from what he told the Eton Park group.

sources.title: How Paulson Gave Hedge Funds Advance Word of Fannie Mae Rescue

facts.claim: Other attendees named in the report included Stephen Mandel of Lone Pine, Dinakar Singh of TPG-Axon and Daniel Och of Och-Ziff.

sources.title: How Paulson gave hedge funds advance word

facts.claim: William Black, a former general counsel at the Federal Home Loan Bank of San Francisco, said 'There were no legitimate reasons for those disclosures'; Bloomberg View columnist William Cohan wrote that the conversation was not a crime, while questioning whether it amounted to 'crony capitalism'.
facts.quote: There were no legitimate reasons for those disclosures.

openQuestions: Site claim that Paulson 'explicitly warned' attendees of the conservatorship plan: Bloomberg's account, from one attendee, says he described conservatorship as a possible path; the site's wording is stronger than the source.

Site claim that attendees 'shorted Fannie and Freddie shares to pennies, capturing billions': no source returned documents any attendee's trades. Bloomberg's report does not establish that anyone traded on the information.
Site claim that no charges were brought: consistent with the coverage returned, but no official statement closing an inquiry was found.
